questions.question: Which description of a functional interface matches the lecture?
options: An interface with no methods at all, used only as a marker
An interface with exactly one abstract method; it may also contain default and static methods
An interface whose methods are all static, so they can be called without an object
Any interface that is annotated with `@FunctionalInterface`, whatever methods it has
questions.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (like `compareTo` in Comparable or `compare` in Comparator); default and static methods are allowed because they already have bodies. That single abstract method is what a lambda implements. The annotation only asks the compiler to check the rule — it does not make an interface with two abstract methods functional.

questions.question: Using the lecture's `Student(name, rollNo, marks)` class, what order are the names printed in?
options: Aditya, Rohan, Rohit, Sonu
Sonu, Rohan, Rohit, Aditya
Sonu, Rohit, Rohan, Aditya
Aditya, Rohit, Rohan, Sonu
questions.explanation: Swapping the operands (`s2` vs `s1`) reverses the natural String order, so names come out in descending lexicographic order. "Rohit" and "Rohan" share "Roh"; then 'i' > 'a', so Rohit is greater and comes before Rohan in descending order. "Aditya, Rohan, Rohit, Sonu" is the ascending result of `s1.name.compareTo(s2.name)`.

questions.question: The teacher wants students by marks, the admin by name and the office by roll number. `Student` is a plain class that you prefer not to change. Which call sorts by roll number using the lecture's approach?
options: `Collections.sort(list, new SortByRollNo());` where `SortByRollNo implements Comparator<Student>`
`Collections.sort(list);` after adding a second `compareTo` method to Student for roll numbers
`Collections.sort(new SortByRollNo());` without passing the list
`list.sortByRollNo();`, which every List provides automatically
questions.explanation: Comparator keeps the ordering logic outside the class: each `SortByX` class implements `compare(Student s1, Student s2)`, and you pass the one you want to `Collections.sort(list, comparator)`. A class cannot have two `compareTo(Student)` methods with the same signature, and the one-argument `Collections.sort(list)` only works with Comparable elements anyway.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts `Comparable` and `Comparator`?
options: Comparable is used by TreeSet, Comparator only by lists; otherwise they are identical
Comparator's method is `compareTo(T o)` and Comparable's is `compare(T o1, T o2)`
Comparable can be written as a lambda, Comparator cannot because it has default methods
Comparable's `compareTo(T o)` lives inside the class and defines its single natural order; Comparator's `compare(T o1, T o2)` lives outside and you can write many of them
questions.explanation: Comparable is implemented by the class itself ("I know how to compare myself"), giving one natural ordering through `compareTo(T o)`. Comparator is a separate object comparing two instances via `compare(T o1, T o2)`, so you can have SortByName, SortByMarks, SortByRollNo, etc. The second option swaps the method names, and default methods do not stop Comparator from being a functional interface.

questions.question: Given the lecture's `Calculate` interface, which line does NOT compile?
options: Line 1
Line 2
Line 3
Line 4
questions.explanation: With a single expression after `->` (Line 1, Line 4) the value is returned implicitly, and explicit parameter types are allowed (Line 4). Once you use braces you write a normal method body, so a value must be returned with `return` (Line 2). Line 3 has braces but no `return`, and `a - b;` is not even a valid statement, so it fails to compile.

questions.question: `Calculate c = (a, b) -> a + b;` compiles, but `Object o = (a, b) -> a + b;` does not. What explains this?
options: A lambda has no type of its own; it takes the type of its target, which must be a functional interface — and Object is not one
Lambdas can only be stored in local variables named after the interface method
Object is a class, and lambdas are always compiled into subclasses of the target type's interface methods only when the parameters are typed
The second line fails only because `a` and `b` have no declared types; writing `(int a, int b)` would fix it
questions.explanation: The compiler works out what a lambda means from the current context (target typing): the target must be a functional interface whose single abstract method the lambda implements, which also gives `a` and `b` their types. Object has no abstract method to implement, so there is nothing to map the lambda to. Adding parameter types does not help, because the target is still not a functional interface.

questions.question:
A teammate has this anonymous class and wants to replace it with a lambda that behaves the same:

`Collections.sort(list, new Comparator<Student>() { public int compare(Student s1, Student s2) { return s1.name.compareTo(s2.name); } });`

Which replacement is correct?
options: `Collections.sort(list, s -> s.name);`
`Collections.sort(list, (s1, s2) -> s1.name.compareTo(s2.name));`
`Collections.sort(list, (s1, s2) -> s1.name == s2.name);`
`Collections.sort(list, (s1, s2) -> s1.name.length() - s2.name.length());`
questions.explanation: The lambda must match `int compare(Student, Student)`: two parameters, an int result. `(s1, s2) -> s1.name.compareTo(s2.name)` is exactly the anonymous class's body without the boilerplate. The one-parameter version has the wrong shape and `==` returns a boolean, so neither compiles; the `length()` version compiles but sorts by name length, not alphabetically.

questions.question: A teammate writes `interface Task { void start(); void stop(); }` and then `Task t = () -> System.out.println("Hello");`, which fails to compile. Which change lets the lambda line compile while keeping both methods on `Task`?
options: Add `@FunctionalInterface` above `Task`
Add explicit parameter types to the lambda: `(void) -> ...`
Make `Task` an abstract class instead of an interface
Give `stop()` a body by making it a `default` method, so `start()` is the only abstract method
questions.explanation: A lambda can only target an interface with exactly one abstract method; with `start()` and `stop()` both abstract, the compiler cannot know which one the lambda implements. A `default` method has a body and does not count, so `Task` becomes functional. `@FunctionalInterface` would just turn the problem into a compile error on the interface, and lambdas can never target abstract classes.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: HI RAM | Dear Sita
HI RAM | Hi Sita
DEAR RAM | Dear Sita
Compilation error: a functional interface cannot have default or static methods
questions.explanation: Greeter has one abstract method (`greet`), so it is a valid functional interface; the default and static methods don't count. `g.loud("ram")` calls g's own `greet` → "Hi ram" and upper-cases it → "HI RAM". `Greeter.polite()` returns a different lambda object, so its `greet("Sita")` gives "Dear Sita" — each lambda carries its own implementation of `greet`, which is why "Hi Sita" and "DEAR RAM" are wrong.

questions.question: In `Collections.sort(list, (s1, s2) -> s1.marks - s2.marks);` with `list` a `List<Student>`, what actually happens?
options: The lambda is compiled into a new method inside the Student class, which `sort` calls by name
`s1` and `s2` are of type Object, so the code only compiles because `marks` is a public field
The lambda becomes an object implementing `Comparator<Student>` (its body is `compare`), with `s1`/`s2` inferred as Student from the context, and `sort` calls it whenever it compares two elements
The lambda runs once before sorting and its single result decides ascending or descending order
questions.explanation: Java passes behaviour by wrapping the "how" in a box — an object implementing a functional interface. The second parameter of `sort` is a Comparator, so by target typing the lambda implements `compare(Student, Student)` and the parameter types are inferred as Student. `sort` invokes that `compare` many times during the sort; it does not run once, and nothing is added to Student.
